hints: Think about how an aromatic amine can be converted into a very good leaving group. What unstable nitrogen-containing cation is formed from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ at low temperature?
Recall what happens when that diazonium intermediate is warmed in aqueous solution, and what temperature control is needed for the two stages.
walkthrough:
Make the diazonium salt first**
You cannot replace $\text{-NH}_2$ by $\text{-OH}$ directly. Sit with phenylamine and picture converting the $\text{-NH}_2$ group into $\text{-N}_2^+$, which leaves as stable $\text{N}_2$ gas very easily. That is diazotisation. Use sodium nitrite plus hydrochloric acid, which makes nitrous acid $\text{HNO}_2$ in situ, and keep the mixture very cold, below $10^{\circ}\text{C}$, typically $0$ to $5^{\circ}\text{C}$, so the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ does not decompose.

Hydrolyse by warming with water**
Now warm that benzenediazonium chloride solution with water. Heating above about $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ lets water act as the nucleophile, $\text{N}_2$ bubbles off and you get phenol. So the two conditions to quote are cold $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ followed by warm aqueous solution.

Final answer: $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl (aq)}$ (forms $\text{HNO}_2$) at $T < 10^{\circ}\text{C}$ to form $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+$.
Then warm with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ with $T \geqslant 10^{\circ}\text{C}$ to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}^+$.

hints: Remember phenol is enormously activated toward electrophilic substitution, so even dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature can nitrate without concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Recall where the $\text{-OH}$ group directs incoming electrophiles, and use the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_3$ to work out how many $\text{NO}_2$ groups have been added.
walkthrough:
See why mild nitration works**
The lone pair on the phenolic oxygen is delocalised into the ring, making the ring very electron rich. That means phenol does not need the powerful nitrating mixture of concentrated $\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. Dilute aqueous $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature is enough for mononitration.

Place the nitro group ortho and para**
$\text{-OH}$ is 2,4-directing. The formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_3$ corresponds to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{OH})(\text{NO}_2)$, so only one $\text{NO}_2$ has entered. The two isomers are therefore 2-nitrophenol with $\text{NO}_2$ next to $\text{OH}$, and 4-nitrophenol with $\text{NO}_2$ opposite $\text{OH}$.

Final answer: Products are 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.
Structures: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and one $\text{NO}_2$ group ortho to $\text{OH}$; benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and one $\text{NO}_2$ group para to $\text{OH}$.

hints: Think about how many positions are strongly activated in phenol when excess bromine water is present, compared to benzene which needs $\text{FeBr}_3$.
Remember to number the ring starting from the $\text{OH}$ as position 1 to name the fully brominated product.
walkthrough:
Brominate all three activated positions**
Picture phenol with $\text{OH}$ at the top. Positions 2, 4 and 6, that is two ortho plus one para, are all highly activated. With excess aqueous bromine, substitution happens at all three without any catalyst, giving a ring with $\text{OH}$ plus three $\text{Br}$ atoms.

Name from the OH group**
Always give $\text{OH}$ carbon number 1 in phenol. Going round the ring, the bromines sit at 2, 4 and 6, so the systematic name is 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

Final answer: Structure: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at positions 2, 4 and 6.
Name: 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

hints: Recall the colour of aqueous bromine and what happens to that colour when bromine is consumed, plus the physical state of the tribromo product.
walkthrough:
Link colour change to solid formation**
Aqueous bromine is orange. As $\text{Br}_2$ is used up in substitution it loses that colour. At the same time the organic product, 2,4,6-tribromophenol, is insoluble in water and appears as a white solid. You must state both observations together for the classic phenol test.
Final answer: Orange bromine water is decolourised AND a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed.

hints: Think of phenol as $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ donating its $\text{OH}$ proton to a strong alkali such as $\text{NaOH}$, just like a carboxylic acid would.
walkthrough:
Write phenol acting as a proton donor**
Think of the $\text{O-H}$ in phenol giving $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{OH}^-$ from sodium hydroxide. That makes water plus the conjugate base sodium phenoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$. Balance is 1:1, and state symbols are not required but the formulae and charges must be correct.

hints: Compare the ability of each compound to lose $\text{H}^+$ by thinking about how stable the resulting anion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, $\text{OH}^-$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ would be.
Consider what happens to the lone pair on oxygen in phenol and in the phenoxide ion, versus the effect of the ethyl group pushing electrons toward oxygen in ethanol.
Link anion stability to how easily the original $\text{O-H}$ bond releases $\text{H}^+$, to order phenol, water and ethanol from most to least acidic.
walkthrough:
State the acidity order**
Acidity means ease of losing $\text{H}^+$. The correct order starting with the most acidic is phenol, then water, then ethanol as the least acidic: $\text{phenol} > \text{water} > \text{ethanol}$.

Explain why phenol is strongest**
Look at phenol and its anion. In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, the negative charge and a lone pair on oxygen can be delocalised into the pi system of the benzene ring. That spreading of charge stabilises the phenoxide ion. A more stable conjugate base means the parent $\text{O-H}$ bond is weaker and $\text{H}^+$ is donated more readily than from water.

Explain why ethanol is weakest**
Now look at ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The ethyl group pushes electron density toward oxygen by the positive inductive effect. In the ethoxide ion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$, that extra electron density intensifies the negative charge on oxygen and destabilises the anion. The $\text{O-H}$ bond is therefore stronger and $\text{H}^+$ is lost even less easily than from water.

Final answer: phenol > water > ethanol (most to least acidic).
In phenol, the lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the benzene ring, stabilising the phenoxide ion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ and weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond, so $\text{H}^+$ is lost more easily.
In ethanol, the ethyl group has a positive inductive (electron donating) effect which destabilises the ethoxide ion $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, strengthening the $\text{O-H}$ bond, so $\text{H}^+$ is lost less easily than from water.
